message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
The pilot gives Cabinet something we rarely have in local climate policy: a clear before-and-after comparison with the rest of the county acting as a benchmark. Installations in the pilot districts rose by 70% against 20% elsewhere, a gap that is far too large to be chance, and households themselves told us the top-up was important in their decision. That is strong evidence the grant works. The value-for-money case is equally robust. Using standard carbon savings per installation and a conservative 15-year life, the Council paid about £56 per tonne, less than half its own £120 appraisal threshold. We have deliberately kept the design the same as the pilot, same grant level, same eligibility, same payment route, so we are scaling something proven rather than experimenting. The risks around installer capacity and national policy are real but manageable, and we have mitigations for each. I am confident this is one of the most cost-effective climate measures available to the Council.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Policy Brief: Extending the Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Countywide
Climate and Environment Team, Harnley County Council, June 2026

1. Recommendation
That Cabinet extend the £2,500 local top-up grant for domestic heat pumps, piloted in two districts in 2025, to the whole county from April 2027, with a budget of £2.5 million a year for an initial two years.

2. Background
Domestic heating accounts for around a quarter of the county's carbon emissions, and most homes are heated by gas or oil boilers. The national boiler upgrade grant covers part of the cost of a heat pump, but survey evidence shows the remaining upfront cost is still the main barrier for households, with typical net costs of £4,000 to £7,000 after the national grant.

In January 2025 the Council launched a local top-up of £2,500 per installation in Ashby and Coleton districts, paid on top of the national grant. The top-up was available to owner-occupiers only, with the installation carried out by an accredited installer. The pilot ran for the full calendar year.

3. Results
Table 1. Heat pump installations, by district group
District group | 2024 installations | 2025 installations | Change
Pilot districts (Ashby, Coleton) | 140 | 238 | +70%
Other five districts | 210 | 252 | +20%
County total | 350 | 490 | +40%

Installations in the pilot districts grew by 70%, compared with 20% elsewhere. The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth, and we expect a similar uplift in the remaining districts once the top-up is available countywide.

The pilot also had broader benefits. In March 2025 the regional installer training centre opened at Coleton College, and the number of accredited installers based in the two pilot districts rose from 9 to 23 over the year. Installers reported that the top-up gave them the confidence to recruit. Wait times for an installation survey in the pilot districts fell from around ten weeks to four.

Customer feedback was positive: of 196 households who completed the follow-up survey, 88% were satisfied or very satisfied with their heat pump, and 91% said the top-up was important in their decision.

4. Value for money
Grant payments in the pilot totalled £595,000 (238 installations at £2,500). Each heat pump replacing a gas or oil boiler saves about 2.1 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, so the 238 installations will save around 500 tonnes a year, or 7,500 tonnes over a 15-year equipment life. That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne, well below the £120 per tonne threshold the Council uses to appraise climate investments.

5. Proposal
We propose a countywide top-up of £2,500 per installation, with the same eligibility and installer requirements as the pilot, capped at 1,000 grants a year (£2.5 million). On current trends, demand is likely to reach this cap in the first year. Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers, we expect demand from the private rented sector to remain a significant share of applications, which supports the Council's private-sector housing standards objectives.

Administration would continue to be handled by the existing two-person grants team, with one additional post funded separately from the Council's climate reserve. Grants would be paid directly to installers on completion, as in the pilot, to reduce the risk of fraud.

6. Risks
Installer capacity outside the pilot districts is lower, and waiting lists could lengthen if demand rises sharply. We will work with the training centre to promote accreditation in other districts.
If the national grant is reduced, the local top-up may be insufficient on its own to sustain demand. We will review the scheme annually.

7. Conclusion
The pilot shows that a modest local top-up substantially increases heat pump uptake, at a cost per tonne of carbon well within the Council's threshold. Extending it countywide is a cost-effective way to accelerate the decarbonisation of home heating.
</document>
response:
# Review: Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Policy Brief

The recommendation is clear: £2,500 top-up, countywide, from April 2027, £2.5m a year for two years. **The brief is not ready for Cabinet.** The value-for-money figure is miscalculated and also measured on the wrong basis. The causal claim has an obvious confounder that the brief itself reports. And the proposal contradicts itself on eligibility. Each of these is fixable, but corrected, the cost-per-tonne case may not hold.

## Must fix before submission

**1. The £56/tonne figure is an arithmetic error.**
£595,000 ÷ 7,500 tonnes = **about £79/tonne**, not £56. That is still under £120 on the brief's own method, but a Cabinet paper with a wrong headline number will lose credibility once someone checks it.

**2. Value for money counts every installation, not the extra ones.**
The calculation credits the grant with all 238 pilot installations. Many of those households would have installed anyway. The pilot districts had 140 installations in 2024. At the 20% growth seen elsewhere, they would have had about 168 in 2025 without the grant. That leaves about **70 additional installations**.

Even if the grant caused all of that uplift:
- 70 × 2.1 t × 15 years ≈ 2,200 tonnes
- £595,000 ÷ 2,200 t ≈ **£270/tonne**, more than double the £120 threshold.

This needs to be addressed directly. The current brief would lead Cabinet to the opposite conclusion from its own data. The 91% who said the top-up was "important" does not settle the question. Stated importance is not the same as "would not have installed without it." The survey also covers 196 of 238 households, and those who responded may be the more positive ones.

**3. The 50-point uplift cannot be credited to the grant alone.**
The brief states that the top-up "therefore caused" the extra growth. Yet section 3 also reports three other changes, all concentrated in the pilot districts:
- a regional installer training centre opened at Coleton in March 2025;
- accredited installers in the pilot districts rose from 9 to 23;
- survey wait times fell from ten weeks to four.

These are plausible causes of higher installations in their own right. The brief presents them as "broader benefits" of the grant, but the only evidence for that is installers' own reports. Also:
- the numbers are small (a base of 140);
- there is only one comparison year, so earlier trends are unknown;
- there is no test of statistical significance.

The author's note says the gap is "far too large to be chance." That claim is not supported in the document, and chance is not the main concern anyway; the confounding is. Section 3 also says "we expect a similar uplift" elsewhere. That holds only if the other districts also get the installer growth, which section 6 says they lack.

**4. Eligibility is contradictory.**
- Section 2: the pilot was "available to owner-occupiers only."
- Section 5: "the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers."

The proposal uses "the same eligibility as the pilot," so Cabinet cannot tell what it is approving. The private-rented-sector benefit claimed in section 5 depends entirely on which statement is correct. This also bears on the author's point that the design is "the same as the pilot."

## Should fix

**5. The forecast of reaching the 1,000-grant cap is unsupported.**
The county total in 2025 was 490. Applying 70% growth to the non-pilot districts (252 → ~430) and keeping the pilot districts at ~240 gives roughly 670, well short of 1,000. Either show the basis for the forecast or revise it. This matters because the annual cost scales with take-up.

**6. Administration costs are left out of the value-for-money case.**
The extra post is funded from the climate reserve, but it is still a cost of the scheme and should be included. The brief should also explain how the team, plus one post, will handle up to four times the pilot volume.

**7. The risk mitigations are thin.**
"Work with the training centre" and "review annually" are not real mitigations. Installer capacity is likely the main driver of the pilot's results, so it deserves a concrete plan. The national-grant risk would benefit from a stated trigger, such as pausing or adjusting the top-up if the national grant falls by a set amount.

## Minor

- The 2.1 t/year saving is applied to both gas and oil replacements. Oil replacements save more, so state the mix or the source of the figure.
- "Survey evidence" in section 2 needs a citation.
- Section 7 ("substantially increases uptake… well within threshold") should be rewritten once points 1–3 are resolved.

## Suggested way forward

Recalculate value for money on an additional-installations basis and present a range of scenarios. Acknowledge the training-centre confounder openly. Fix the eligibility statement. If the honest cost per tonne lands above £120, the brief could still argue for the scheme on other grounds: market-building, installer capacity, or private-rented-sector standards. It could also propose a better-targeted design, such as lower-income households or oil-heated homes, where the grant is more likely to change behaviour. Cabinet will trust the paper more if it makes that case openly than if it relies on the current figure.
